title: The open enrollment survival kit for HR teams
summary: Make open enrollment easier for your HR team with practical tips to reduce employee questions, improve communication, and prevent last-minute issues.
body_markdown:
"Wait, when is the deadline?" "Which plan should I pick?" "Can I add my spouse later?"


If you work in HR, you've probably answered some version of these questions more times than you can count this open enrollment season.


For employers with January 1 plan years, November and early December can be particularly demanding. Employees who have been putting off their benefits decisions suddenly have questions, deadlines are approaching, and your team is managing enrollment alongside payroll, onboarding, and everything else on its plate.


At Healia, our Account Management team works closely with employers throughout open enrollment. We know how much work goes into preparing employees to make their benefits elections, especially when the same questions keep coming up and deadlines are getting closer.


We've found that some of the most effective ways to make open enrollment easier for HR also make it easier for employees to understand their options and take action. Here are 5 practical ways to reduce the workload on your team during the final weeks of enrollment.


## 1. Fewer repetitive questions start with better information


By this point in open enrollment, you've probably noticed a pattern in the questions employees are asking. Some want to understand the difference between a deductible and an out-of-pocket maximum. Others are trying to figure out whether their spouse can join their plan or what happens if they miss the enrollment deadline.


Your team has likely answered many of these questions individually, often several times. Bringing those answers together in one place can save your team hours of repetitive work.


Start with the 10 questions you've received most frequently this season and create a short, plain-language FAQ. Include examples that explain unfamiliar benefits terminology and make the document easy to find through your benefits portal, company chat, or enrollment emails.


According to the[Employee Benefit Research Institute's 2025 Consumer Engagement in Health Care Survey](https://www.ebri.org/health/publications/fast-facts/content/full/2025-consumer-engagement-in-health-care-survey) , about half of enrollees spent less than an hour choosing a health plan. Employees are making an important financial decision with relatively little time spent evaluating their options, which makes accessible information particularly useful.


Even with a strong FAQ, some employees will need individual support. Offering a few scheduled office hours each week gives them a predictable opportunity to ask questions without interrupting your team's entire day.


If you work with benefits partners who provide employee support, make sure employees know how to reach them. At Healia, for example, our team is available to help employees understand the Total Care Option and compare their healthcare coverage options.


The easier it is for employees to find answers or reach the right person, the fewer questions end up back in your inbox.


## 2. Better communication means fewer last-minute scrambles


Every HR team knows the frustration of sending an important benefits announcement, only to hear from employees weeks later who never saw it.


During open enrollment, employees receive a lot of information in a short period. Some will read every email. Others may miss the first announcement entirely or put off reviewing their options until the deadline is days away.


That creates more work for your team as enrollment closes, particularly when employees need help understanding a benefit or completing their elections.


A consistent communication schedule can help spread that activity across the enrollment period.


We recommend using several channels to reach employees, including email, benefits portals, manager reminders, and printed materials where appropriate. Keep the language simple and focus on what employees need to know: what the benefit does, why it might matter to them, and what they should do next.


As the deadline approaches, schedule a short sequence of reminders rather than relying on one final announcement.


A[2026 Selerix survey](https://selerix.com/blog/selerix-survey-2026/) found that 41% of employees planned to return to a benefits message but never did.


Consider sending reminders 5 days before enrollment closes, again 2 days before, and once more on the final day. Each message should clearly state the deadline and provide a direct link to the enrollment portal.


It's also worth explaining what happens if employees take no action. Some elections may carry forward automatically, while others require an active decision. Clarifying those rules early can prevent confusion and urgent requests after enrollment closes.


A little planning on the communication side can save your team a considerable amount of work when the deadline arrives.


## 3. Helping spouses participate means fewer complicated coverage questions


Some of the most complicated enrollment questions come from employees whose spouses also have access to health insurance through work.


These families may be comparing plans from two employers, each with different premiums, deductibles, provider networks, and enrollment deadlines. Often, the employee is trying to make that comparison without having all the information about their spouse's coverage.


For HR teams, that can lead to lengthy individual conversations about which plan an employee should choose, whether switching to a spouse's plan makes sense, or how different enrollment periods affect their options.


Encouraging employees to involve their spouses earlier can make those conversations easier.


Provide benefits materials that employees can share at home, including plan summaries, enrollment deadlines, and instructions for accessing plan documents. If you have a decision support tool available, encourage employees to compare their household's options before making their elections.


This is especially important because the plan with the lowest monthly premium isn't always the one that costs a family the least over the course of the year. Comparing total healthcare costs can help employees understand their options before turning to HR for guidance.


For employers offering a spousal HRA, there's an additional consideration. Employees may qualify for financial support when they enroll in a spouse's employer-sponsored health plan, but they need to understand how the benefit works and whether it makes sense for their household.


Healia's Decision Support Tool helps employees compare coverage across both employers. Employees can invite their spouse to participate, upload their spouse's plan information, or start with an estimate if they don't have all the documents available.


Giving families a way to evaluate their options independently can reduce the amount of individualized guidance HR teams need to provide.


For more ideas on involving spouses, read[Open enrollment has a plus-one](https://healiahealth.com/blog/open-enrollment-has-a-plus-one) .


## 4. Clear guidance now prevents questions after enrollment closes


One of the easiest ways to create more work for your team in January is to leave employees uncertain about what happens after open enrollment.


Questions about qualifying life events, missed deadlines, and coverage changes can continue long after the enrollment window closes.


Employees may wonder whether they can change their plan after getting married, having a child, or losing other coverage. Those whose spouses have different open enrollment periods may have additional questions about when changes are permitted.


Addressing these situations before the deadline can reduce confusion later.


Include a short explanation of qualifying life events in your enrollment materials, along with instructions for requesting a coverage change and the applicable deadlines.


Under federal law, employees generally have at least 30 days following certain qualifying events, including marriage, birth, adoption, or loss of other coverage, to request special enrollment in an employer-sponsored group health plan. The[U.S. Department of Labor](https://www.dol.gov/node/63429) provides guidance, but employers should confirm the specific rules and procedures in their plan documents.


Make sure employees know where to find this information and who to contact when their circumstances change.


A few clear instructions today can prevent weeks of unnecessary back-and-forth later.


## 5. Better visibility during enrollment means fewer surprises at the end


When you're managing open enrollment, it's helpful to know whether employees are engaging with their benefits information before the deadline arrives.


Unfortunately, final enrollment data isn't always available right away. Depending on your systems and vendors, it may take weeks after enrollment closes to get a complete picture of participation.


Waiting for those results means missing the chance to address problems while employees can still act.


We encourage employers to pay attention to activity throughout the enrollment period. Look at how many employees are visiting your benefits resources, using plan comparison tools, attending information sessions, or reaching out for support.


These indicators can help you identify where additional communication may be needed.


If employees aren't engaging with a particular benefit, for example, you might send a more targeted reminder, ask managers to reinforce the message, or schedule another information session.


This also gives you a better starting point for next year's enrollment planning.


Once enrollment closes, set aside time for a short team debrief. Review which questions came up most often, where employees needed extra help, and which communications were most effective.


Documenting those lessons while they're fresh can save your team time when the next enrollment season begins.


## A little less work for HR, a better experience for employees


Open enrollment will always require coordination, communication, and plenty of employee support. But the more you can help employees find answers, understand their options, and make decisions independently, the more manageable the process becomes for your team.
